title: Beauty inventory management: shades, expiry, and launches
summary: Beauty inventory management sets stock by product role, shade, and expiry window. US prestige beauty grew 4% to $36B in 2025: here is how to plan the stock.
body_markdown:
**By Elie Dufeu, CTO & Co-Founder, Metreecs.** Published 16 November 2026.


Beauty inventory management means deciding how much of each product, shade, and size to hold in each warehouse, store, and partner channel, so that bestsellers stay available while slow shades, launches, and limited editions don't expire on the shelf. It works when stock is planned by product role, when order sizes are checked against the product's sellable window, and when stock held at retailers and marketplaces is counted as part of the same plan.


Nadia runs operations for a skincare and color cosmetics brand sold through its own website, 120 doors at two beauty retailers, and a marketplace store. Her warehouse report says the brand holds nine months of stock overall, which looks comfortable. Yet the bestselling serum is on backorder at one retailer, 14 foundation shades sit at more than two years of cover, and a holiday gift set from last year is still in the stockroom with eight months left before its date. (Nadia is an illustrative example, but most beauty planners will recognize the picture.)


Total stock is rarely the issue. The trouble sits in how that stock is spread across shades, channels, and batches. This guide covers how beauty inventory management differs from other categories, how to set stock rules by product role, how to check minimum order quantities against expiry, how to handle launches and limited editions, and how to keep partner stock in view. If you'd like to see the approach applied to your own range, you can[walk through your shade and channel data with our team](https://www.metreecs.com/form/discover) .


**Key Takeaways**


- US prestige beauty dollar sales grew 4% to $36 billion in 2025 and mass beauty grew 5% to $72.7 billion, according to Circana, so demand is growing while ranges keep widening.
- Under EU Regulation 1223/2009, a cosmetic product with a minimum durability of 30 months or less must carry a date of minimum durability, which turns shelf life into a hard limit on how long stock can wait.
- In a worked example below, a slow shade bought at a 3,000-unit minimum loses 2,370 units to expiry, while a 1,000-unit run at a higher unit cost brings the cost per unit sold from €10.00 down to €5.40 (our own illustrative arithmetic).
- McKinsey found that early adopters of AI-enabled supply chain management improved inventory levels by 35% and service levels by 65% compared with slower competitors.


## What is beauty inventory management?


Beauty inventory management is the planning and control of stock for skincare, makeup, fragrance, hair, and body products across warehouses, own stores, retail partners, and online channels. It sets order quantities, reorder timing, and stock per location for each product and variant, within the limits set by shelf life, minimum production runs, and channel rules.


Four features make it harder than planning most consumer goods. The first is the variant explosion: one foundation can come in 40 shades and two sizes, and each shade sells at its own pace. The second is time: every product has a usable life, and retail partners often refuse stock that arrives too close to its date. The third is the launch calendar, since new products, limited editions, and gift sets make up a large share of the year's buying decisions with little or no history to plan from.


The fourth is fragmentation. A brand's stock can sit in its own warehouse, in a third-party logistics site, in partner distribution centers, in stores as testers, and in a marketplace fulfilment network, and each location follows different rules. Circana's 2025 data shows how much the channel mix varies even inside beauty: hair is the only prestige category where online accounts for the majority of sales, so a hair range and a makeup range from the same brand can need very different stock placement.


Demand forecasting is one input to all this, and we cover it in our guide to[demand forecasting for beauty brands](https://www.metreecs.com/blog/demand-forecasting-beauty-brands) , including how shelf life caps days of inventory. This article stays on the inventory side: what to hold, where, and in what batches.


## Plan beauty inventory management by product role


A single stock rule applied to every product is the fastest way to end up short on heroes and long on shades nobody asks for. Grouping the range by role gives each group a rule that fits how it sells.


Product roleExamplesStock ruleMain riskHero productsBestselling serum, core mascara, signature fragranceContinuous replenishment with safety stock, highest availability targetStockouts at partners and online, which push shoppers to substitutesShade and size rangesFoundation, concealer, lipstick shades, travel sizesForecast at range level, split by shade mix, cap cover by expirySlow shades bought at minimum runs that outlast their datesLaunchesNew skincare line, new fragrancePhased buy: initial quantity plus a reserve on components or open production slotsOverbuying on launch hype, or missing the first reorderLimited editions and gift setsHoliday sets, seasonal palettes, collaborationsOne buy, no reorder, planned exit date and clearance pathLeftovers that can't be sold after the seasonTesters and samplesStore testers, gift-with-purchase minisPlanned as a cost per door, not as sales stockTester stock drawn from sellable stock without a record


Hero products deserve the tightest control because they carry the brand's revenue and its relationship with partners. A missing hero at a retailer costs the sale and often the shelf space, since buyers watch out-of-stock rates by brand.


Shade ranges need a different logic. Forecasting each shade on its own produces noisy numbers for the pale and deep ends of a range, where weekly sales are tiny. A steadier approach forecasts the whole range and splits it by the recent shade mix, then checks each shade's order against its expiry window (the next section shows how).


Across Metreecs' work with beauty brands, the shade range is where most of the slow stock hides, because ranges are extended at launch and rarely trimmed afterwards. Reviewing the bottom fifth of each range twice a year, and moving the slowest shades to online only, keeps the store assortment honest without removing the shade for the customers who need it.


## Expiry, minimum orders, and the sellable window


Most beauty inventory management problems come down to a mismatch between how much a supplier must make and how much the market can sell before the date. Contract manufacturers and fillers usually set minimum batch sizes, and components such as printed cartons or custom compacts often have their own minimums. Those terms are usually agreed at launch and rarely revisited.


In the EU, Regulation 1223/2009 makes the date of minimum durability mandatory for any cosmetic with a minimum durability of 30 months or less, while longer-life products carry a period-after-opening mark instead. Many partners also set a minimum remaining life at delivery. That gives each product a sellable window: the time between production and the latest date a unit can still reach a customer.


Here is a worked example with our own illustrative numbers.


- A lipstick shade sells 30 units a month across all channels.
- It has a 24-month shelf life, and the brand stops selling units with less than three months left, so the sellable window is 21 months.
- Over 21 months, the shade can sell about 630 units.
- Option A: the filler's minimum run is 3,000 units at €2.10 each, so €6,300 in total. About 2,370 units expire unsold. The cost per unit actually sold is €6,300 / 630 = €10.00.
- Option B: a 1,000-unit run at €3.40 each, so €3,400. About 370 units expire. The cost per unit sold is €3,400 / 630 = €5.40.


The higher unit price looks worse on a purchase order, yet it nearly halves the real cost of each unit sold. The test to run before every order is simple: divide the order quantity by forecast monthly demand, compare it with the sellable window, and price the expected write-off before signing.


When neither option works, the remaining choices are commercial ones. The brand can share a bulk batch across several shades where the formula allows it, move the shade to a made-to-order or online-only model, or retire it. The planners we work with often underestimate how many shades fail this test, because the minimum run was set when everyone expected the whole range to sell.


Once the stock is in the warehouse, picking order matters too. First-expired, first-out picking keeps the oldest batches moving, and our comparison of[FEFO vs FIFO](https://www.metreecs.com/blog/fefo-vs-fifo) explains when each rule fits.


## Launches, limited editions, and testers


Launches and limited editions are where beauty inventory management gets the most attention and the least history. A new product has no sales record, so the first buy rests on comparable products, pre-orders, and the marketing plan. Forecasting methods for new products deserve their own guide; the inventory question here is how to structure the buy.


For launches, a phased buy reduces the risk on both sides. The brand commits to an initial quantity that covers the launch window at partners and online, then holds a reserve in a less costly form: bulk that hasn't been filled, components on hand, or a booked production slot. The first two to four weeks of sell-through decide whether the reserve becomes finished goods.


Limited editions need the opposite discipline. They get one buy, with no reorder, so the plan should state the exit date and the clearance route before the order is placed. Grace plans a holiday gift set for a fragrance brand. She buys 8,000 sets for an eight-week window and agrees in advance that any stock left on 10 January moves to the brand's outlet and staff sales, with a fixed markdown. When 1,100 sets remain in January, the decision is already made and the stock is gone within a month instead of sitting in the warehouse until its date. (Grace is also an illustrative example.)


Testers and samples are the quiet leak. They are often pulled from sellable stock in stores without a transaction, so the system shows units that no longer exist and the replenishment logic under-orders. Recording testers as a planned cost per door, with their own movement type, keeps both the stock and the margin readable.


## Partner stock, marketplaces, and returns


A brand that sells through retailers holds stock it doesn't control: units sitting in partner distribution centers and stores. When partners reorder from their own forecasts, a sales spike can be absorbed by their buffer, and a slowdown can turn into a sudden pause in orders. Beauty inventory management works better when the brand gets sell-out data by door from its partners, not just sell-in orders, and plans its own warehouse against that.


Tomás manages supply for a haircare brand sold in 300 pharmacy and salon doors plus its own site. For a year he planned from partner orders and kept seeing order spikes in March and gaps in May. Once he received weekly sell-out by door, he saw that consumer demand was flat and the spikes came from partners rebuilding stock after inventory counts. He moved to planning on sell-out and agreed target stock levels per door with the two largest partners, which made his own production plan steadier. (Tomás is an illustrative example.)


Marketplaces add another layer: stock sent to a marketplace fulfilment network is out of the brand's warehouse but not yet sold, and it often has its own storage fees and age limits. It should appear in the plan as a separate location, with its own cover target.


Returns close the loop. Returned beauty products are often unsellable for hygiene reasons once opened, so a return can mean a write-off rather than restock. Plan on net demand (sales minus returns that come back to sellable stock) and track the share of returns that are destroyed by channel, because a channel with high destroyed returns needs a smaller safety buffer than its gross sales suggest.


One mistake we repeatedly see is a brand treating everything shipped to partners as sold, then discovering in the next season that the same units come back as returns or markdown requests.


## A monthly beauty inventory management routine


A short, regular cycle catches most problems while they're still cheap to fix. This one fits a brand or retailer with a few hundred to a few thousand variants.


1. **Refresh demand.** Update the forecast for each product role, using sell-out where partners share it and net of returns.
2. **Check cover against expiry.** For every product, compare days of cover with the remaining sellable window of the oldest batch, and flag anything that will not sell in time.
3. **Review open orders.** Test each planned production run against the sellable window, as in the worked example, before it's confirmed.
4. **Rebalance locations.** Move short-dated stock to the channel that sells fastest (often your own site or outlet) and keep longer-dated stock for partners with remaining-life rules.
5. **Plan launches and limited editions.** Confirm reserve quantities for launches and exit dates for limited editions in the next six months.
6. **Decide on the tail.** List shades and sizes below a minimum sales rate and choose for each: keep, move online only, or retire.


In our experience deploying batch-level planning at Metreecs, steps 2 and 4 are where most of the value sits, because they turn expiry from a write-off found at the year-end count into a decision taken months earlier. The same cycle runs on spreadsheets for a small range; once batches, shades, and partner locations multiply,[AI-driven inventory optimization](https://www.metreecs.com/inventory-optimization) keeps the batch-level checks running every week without a manual rebuild.


## FAQ


### How do you manage inventory for a beauty brand?


Group the range by role (heroes, shade ranges, launches, limited editions, testers) and give each group its own stock rule. Track stock by batch with its expiry date, check every production run against the time it will take to sell, and include stock held at retail partners and marketplaces in the same plan. Review the plan monthly.


### How do you track expiry dates on cosmetics?


Record the batch and its date of minimum durability (or production date and shelf life) at receipt, and pick first-expired, first-out. Then go one step further than tracking: compare each batch's remaining life with its forecast sales, so short-dated stock is moved or sold while there is still time.


### How much stock should a beauty brand hold for a launch?


Enough to cover the launch window at partners and online, plus a reserve held in a cheaper form, such as unfilled bulk, components, or a booked production slot. Use the first weeks of sell-through to decide whether to convert the reserve into finished goods. Size the initial buy from comparable launches, not from the marketing target alone.


### What should you do with short-dated or expired beauty products?


Short-dated stock should be moved to the channel that sells fastest, such as your own website, an outlet, or staff sales, before it falls below partners' remaining-life rules. Expired stock can't be sold and must be disposed of in line with local rules. Good beauty inventory management reduces the second group by acting on the first.


### How do you manage inventory for many shades?


Forecast the shade range as a whole and split it by recent shade mix, because single-shade forecasts are noisy at the edges of a range. Cap each shade's order by its sellable window, and review the slowest shades twice a year to decide whether they stay in stores, move online, or are retired.


## Conclusion


Beauty inventory management comes down to three checks: plan each product by its role, size every order against the sellable window, and keep partner and marketplace stock in the same view as your own warehouse. A useful first step is to list every shade whose last production run covers more months than its shelf life allows.
